title: Neo-Elamite Elam
subtitle: 1,100–539 BC · Revival, the Assyrian Wars, and the Destruction of Susa

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Silence, revival, fratricidal collapse, and absorption into rising Persia

entries.label: The Long Silence
entries.hint: Following Nebuchadnezzar I's invasion, royal inscriptions from Elam all but disappear from the record for roughly three centuries — whether from genuine political fragmentation, a simple gap in what has survived to be excavated, or both, historians still debate, but the silence itself is the defining fact of this stretch of Elamite history.
entries.note: The near-total absence of dated Elamite royal inscriptions between the Shutrukid collapse and the Neo-Elamite revival.

entries.label: The Neo-Elamite Revival
entries.hint: Kings such as Humban-tahrah and Shutruk-Nahhunte II reappear in the textual record as Elam re-enters Mesopotamian affairs, rebuilding enough central authority at Susa to matter again in the power politics of an Assyrian-dominated Near East.
entries.note: Assyrian royal annals naming Neo-Elamite kings from the mid-9th century BC onward.

entries.label: Humban-nikash and the Anti-Assyrian Alliance
entries.hint: Humban-nikash allied Elam with the Chaldean leader Marduk-apla-iddina II of Babylon against the Assyrian king Sargon II, establishing the pattern — an Elamite-Babylonian axis against Assyria — that would define Elamite foreign policy for the next century, with consequences that eventually proved catastrophic for Elam itself.
entries.note: Sargon II's annals, on the Elamite-Babylonian alliance and the Battle of Der.

entries.label: Teumman and the Fratricidal Succession Crisis
entries.hint: Teumman seized the Elamite throne and drove out his cousins, who fled to the Assyrian court at Nineveh — Ashurbanipal's decision to back the exiled claimants against Teumman gave Assyria the pretext for direct intervention that would, within a decade, end in Elam's total destruction.
entries.note: Ashurbanipal's annals, on Teumman's usurpation and the Assyrian-backed exiles.

entries.label: Fragments after the Destruction
entries.hint: After Ashurbanipal's sack of Susa, Elamite political authority survived only in scattered, much-reduced petty kingdoms until the rising Persian dynasty based at Anshan — Teispes, Cyrus I, Cambyses I and finally Cyrus II — absorbed the remaining Elamite structures and titulature into what would become the Achaemenid state.
entries.note: Cyrus Cylinder, on Cyrus's own dynastic claims; Elamite administrative continuity evidence at Persepolis and Susa under early Achaemenid rule.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The anti-Assyrian alliances, the Battle of Halule, and the destruction of Susa

entries.label: The Battle of Der
entries.hint: Humban-nikash's Elamite army fought Sargon II's Assyrians to at least a tactical standstill at Der while Marduk-apla-iddina II secured Babylon — both Assyrian and Babylonian sources claim victory, but the battle's practical effect was to keep Babylon out of direct Assyrian control for another decade.
entries.note: Sargon II's annals and the Babylonian Chronicle, giving conflicting accounts of the battle's outcome.

entries.label: The Battle of Halule
entries.hint: A massive, bloody and militarily inconclusive battle between Sennacherib's Assyrian army and a combined Elamite-Babylonian-allied coalition ended with both sides claiming victory in their own inscriptions — one of the largest set-piece battles of the entire Neo-Assyrian period, decisive for neither side in practice.
entries.note: Sennacherib's annals, claiming victory; Babylonian Chronicle, presenting a more equivocal account.

entries.label: The Battle of the Ulai and Teumman's Death
entries.hint: Ashurbanipal's army, accompanied by Teumman's exiled Elamite rivals, decisively defeated and killed Teumman at the Ulai river — a battle so celebrated at Nineveh that Ashurbanipal had its scenes, including Teumman's severed head, carved across an entire palace relief cycle.
entries.note: Ashurbanipal's Til Tuba reliefs, British Museum, depicting the battle and Teumman's death in detail.

entries.label: Ashurbanipal's Destruction of Susa
entries.hint: Ashurbanipal's own inscriptions boast of levelling Susa's ziggurat, desecrating the tombs of past Elamite kings and scattering their bones, looting the temples of Inshushinak, and sowing the ruins with salt — a deliberate, comprehensively documented act of state erasure aimed at ending Elam as a political entity, not merely defeating it in battle.
entries.note: Ashurbanipal's annals (Rassam Cylinder), on the destruction of Susa.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: What little the fragmentary record shows of a declining kingdom's administration

entries.label: A Kingdom Governed for War
entries.hint: What administrative texts survive from the Neo-Elamite period concern themselves overwhelmingly with military mobilisation and alliance management rather than the temple-building and land-grant records that dominate earlier Elamite archives — a state whose surviving bureaucratic footprint reflects a century spent almost continuously mobilising against Assyria.
entries.note: Neo-Elamite administrative tablet fragments, Susa; comparative scarcity against the Sukkalmah and Middle Elamite archives.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Inshushinak's cult surviving a kingdom's collapse

entries.label: Inshushinak's Temple Looted
entries.hint: Ashurbanipal's inscriptions specifically single out the looting of Inshushinak's temple and the removal of its cult statues to Assyria — a calculated act, since destroying a patron god's cult image was itself understood across the ancient Near East as an attack on a kingdom's very legitimacy to exist, not merely on its material wealth.
entries.note: Ashurbanipal's annals (Rassam Cylinder), on the temple of Inshushinak.

entries.label: Elamite Cult Continuity into Persian Rule
entries.hint: Despite the destruction of 646 BC, worship of Inshushinak and other Elamite deities continued at a reduced scale into the early Achaemenid period — Susa's religious life proved considerably harder to erase permanently than Ashurbanipal's inscriptions had boasted, surviving to be absorbed rather than extinguished by the rising Persian state.
entries.note: Elamite religious continuity evidence in early Achaemenid-period Susa and Persepolis administrative texts.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Ashurbanipal's own reliefs, the only detailed visual record of Susa's fall

entries.label: The Til Tuba Reliefs at Nineveh
entries.loc: Found: Nineveh · Now: British Museum, London
entries.hint: Carved for Ashurbanipal's palace at Nineveh, the Til Tuba relief cycle depicts the Battle of the Ulai in vivid narrative detail — Teumman's chariot overturning, his son begging for his life, his severed head displayed at an Assyrian victory feast — the single most detailed visual source for any Elamite military event, made entirely by the enemy that destroyed the subject it depicts.
entries.note: Til Tuba battle reliefs, British Museum (Room 10a).

entries.label: The Sack of Susa Depicted at Nineveh
entries.loc: Found: Nineveh · Now: British Museum, London
entries.hint: A further relief cycle from Ashurbanipal's palace shows Assyrian soldiers demolishing Susa's ziggurat and carrying off statues and temple furnishings — a triumphal Assyrian visual record that, read against the grain, is also the fullest surviving depiction of what a major Elamite city's monumental core actually looked like just before its destruction.
entries.note: Ashurbanipal's Susa campaign reliefs, British Museum.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Elamite language's long terminal decline

entries.label: The Elamite Language's Terminal Decline
entries.hint: Written Elamite becomes progressively rarer across this period, surviving mainly in royal titulature and brief administrative notations rather than the extended building inscriptions of earlier centuries — a linguistic contraction running in parallel with, and likely reinforcing, the kingdom's political fragmentation.
entries.note: Comparative corpus-size analysis of Neo-Elamite versus Middle Elamite textual survival.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: A shrinking kingdom's shrinking resource base

entries.label: A Shrinking Resource Base
entries.hint: Repeated warfare, tribute demands from shifting alliances, and the loss of the Middle Elamite kingdom's old wealth from Babylon meant Neo-Elamite Susa operated on a substantially reduced economic base compared to Shutruk-Nahhunte's era — a kingdom fighting for survival with steadily diminishing resources to fight with.
entries.note: Comparative economic scale inferred from the reduced Neo-Elamite building and administrative record.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Continuity and loss in a declining state

entries.label: The Ziggurat's Deliberate Levelling
entries.hint: Ashurbanipal's forces did not simply loot Susa's ziggurat but deliberately dismantled it — a technical undertaking in its own right, requiring organised demolition labour, aimed at ensuring the structure's religious and political symbolism could not simply be repaired and reused by any future Elamite king.
entries.note: Ashurbanipal's annals, on the ziggurat's demolition; archaeological confirmation of the structure's near-total loss.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Alliances with Babylon against Assyria, and the fragments' absorption

entries.label: The Elamite-Babylonian Axis against Assyria
entries.hint: For roughly a century, successive Elamite kings maintained a diplomatic and military partnership with Chaldean Babylon against their shared Assyrian adversary — an alliance that repeatedly saved Babylon from Assyrian conquest but ultimately failed to save Elam itself, since Assyria could and did deal with each ally separately once it chose to.
entries.note: Assyrian royal annals and the Babylonian Chronicle, documenting the recurring Elamite-Babylonian alliance.

entries.label: Elamite Structures Absorbed into Persia
entries.hint: Rather than being conquered outright, what remained of Elamite political and administrative structure at Anshan and Susa was progressively absorbed by the rising Persian dynasty, whose own kings had held the old Elamite royal title 'King of Anshan' for at least two generations before Cyrus's final unification.
entries.note: Cyrus Cylinder; Elamite-Achaemenid administrative continuity evidence, Persepolis Fortification Archive.
